segs.p: “Anicceyeva, bhikkhave, bhikkhu rūpe aniccāti passati, sāssa hoti sammādiṭṭhi.
segs.e: “Mendicants, sights really are impermanent. A mendicant sees that they are impermanent: that’s their right view.
Seeing rightly, they grow disillusioned.
When relishing ends, greed ends. When greed ends, relishing ends.
When relishing and greed end, the mind is said to be well freed.
Sounds …
Smells …
Tastes …
Touches …

segs.p: dhamme aniccāti passati, sāssa hoti sammādiṭṭhi.
segs.e: Ideas really are impermanent. A mendicant sees that they are impermanent: that’s their right view.
Seeing rightly, they grow disillusioned.
When relishing ends, greed ends. When greed ends, relishing ends.
When relishing and greed end, the mind is said to be well freed.”

16. The End of Relishing
Focus, the Interior, and the End of Relishing

segs.p: “Cakkhuṁ, bhikkhave, yoniso manasi karotha, cakkhāniccatañca yathābhūtaṁ samanupassatha.
segs.e: “Mendicants, rationally apply the mind to the eye. Truly see the impermanence of the eye.

segs.p: Cakkhuṁ, bhikkhave, bhikkhu yoniso manasikaronto, cakkhāniccatañca yathābhūtaṁ samanupassanto cakkhusmimpi nibbindati.
segs.e: When a mendicant does this, they grow disillusioned with the eye.
When relishing ends, greed ends. When greed ends, relishing ends.
When relishing and greed end, the mind is said to be well freed.
Rationally apply the mind to the ear …
nose …

segs.p: jivhaṁ, bhikkhave, yoniso manasi karotha, jivhāniccatañca yathābhūtaṁ samanupassatha.
segs.e: tongue …

segs.p: Jivhaṁ, bhikkhave, bhikkhu yoniso manasikaronto, jivhāniccatañca yathābhūtaṁ samanupassanto jivhāyapi nibbindati.

segs.e: body …

segs.p: manaṁ, bhikkhave, yoniso manasi karotha, manāniccatañca yathābhūtaṁ samanupassatha.
segs.e: mind. Truly see the impermanence of the mind.

segs.p: Manaṁ, bhikkhave, bhikkhu yoniso manasikaronto, manāniccatañca yathābhūtaṁ samanupassanto manasmimpi nibbindati.
segs.e: When a mendicant does this, they grow disillusioned with the mind.
When relishing ends, greed ends. When greed ends, relishing ends.
When relishing and greed end, the mind is said to be well freed.”

segs.p: “Rūpe, bhikkhave, yoniso manasi karotha, rūpāniccatañca yathābhūtaṁ samanupassatha.
segs.e: “Mendicants, rationally apply the mind to sights. Truly see the impermanence of sights.

segs.p: Rūpe, bhikkhave, bhikkhu yoniso manasikaronto, rūpāniccatañca yathābhūtaṁ samanupassanto rūpesupi nibbindati.
segs.e: When a mendicant does this, they grow disillusioned with sights.
When relishing ends, greed ends. When greed ends, relishing ends.
When relishing and greed end, the mind is said to be well freed.
Rationally apply the mind to sounds …
smells …
tastes …
touches …

segs.p: dhamme, bhikkhave, yoniso manasi karotha, dhammāniccatañca yathābhūtaṁ samanupassatha.
segs.e: ideas. Truly see the impermanence of ideas.

segs.p: Dhamme, bhikkhave, bhikkhu yoniso manasikaronto, dhammāniccatañca yathābhūtaṁ samanupassanto dhammesupi nibbindati.
segs.e: When a mendicant does this, they grow disillusioned with ideas.
When relishing ends, greed ends.
When greed ends, relishing ends.
When relishing and greed end, the mind is said to be well freed.”

16. The End of Relishing
On Immersion at Jīvaka’s Mango Grove

segs.p: Ekaṁ samayaṁ bhagavā rājagahe viharati jīvakambavane.
segs.e: At one time the Buddha was staying near Rājagaha in Jīvaka’s Mango Grove.
There the Buddha addressed the mendicants:
“Mendicants, develop immersion.
For a mendicant with immersion, things become truly clear.
And what becomes truly clear?

segs.p: Cakkhuṁ aniccanti yathābhūtaṁ okkhāyati, rūpā aniccāti yathābhūtaṁ okkhāyati, cakkhuviññāṇaṁ aniccanti yathābhūtaṁ okkhāyati, cakkhusamphasso aniccoti yathābhūtaṁ okkhāyati, yampidaṁ cakkhusamphassapaccayā uppajjati vedayitaṁ sukhaṁ vā dukkhaṁ vā adukkhamasukhaṁ vā tampi aniccanti yathābhūtaṁ okkhāyati …pe…
segs.e: It becomes truly clear that the eye, sights, eye consciousness, and eye contact are impermanent. And it also becomes truly clear that the painful, pleasant, or neutral feeling that arises dependent on eye contact is impermanent.
It becomes truly clear that the ear … nose … tongue … body …

segs.p: mano aniccoti yathābhūtaṁ okkhāyati, dhammā aniccāti yathābhūtaṁ okkhāyati …pe…
segs.e: mind, ideas, mind consciousness, and mind contact are impermanent.

segs.p: yampidaṁ manosamphassapaccayā uppajjati vedayitaṁ sukhaṁ vā dukkhaṁ vā adukkhamasukhaṁ vā tampi aniccanti yathābhūtaṁ okkhāyati.
segs.e: And it also becomes truly clear that the painful, pleasant, or neutral feeling that arises dependent on mind contact is impermanent.
Mendicants, develop immersion.
For a mendicant with immersion, things become truly clear.”

16. The End of Relishing
On Retreat at Jīvaka’s Mango Grove

segs.p: Ekaṁ samayaṁ bhagavā rājagahe viharati jīvakambavane.
segs.e: At one time the Buddha was staying near Rājagaha in Jīvaka’s Mango Grove.
There the Buddha addressed the mendicants:
“Mendicants, meditate in retreat.
For a mendicant who meditates in retreat, things become truly clear.
And what becomes truly clear?

segs.p: Cakkhuṁ aniccanti yathābhūtaṁ okkhāyati, rūpā aniccāti yathābhūtaṁ okkhāyati, cakkhuviññāṇaṁ aniccanti yathābhūtaṁ okkhāyati, cakkhusamphasso aniccoti yathābhūtaṁ okkhāyati, yampidaṁ cakkhusamphassapaccayā uppajjati vedayitaṁ sukhaṁ vā dukkhaṁ vā adukkhamasukhaṁ vā tampi aniccanti yathābhūtaṁ okkhāyati …pe…

It becomes truly clear that the mind, ideas, mind consciousness, and mind contact are impermanent.

segs.p: yampidaṁ manosamphassapaccayā uppajjati vedayitaṁ sukhaṁ vā dukkhaṁ vā adukkhamasukhaṁ vā tampi aniccanti yathābhūtaṁ okkhāyati.
segs.e: And it also becomes truly clear that the painful, pleasant, or neutral feeling that arises dependent on mind contact is impermanent.
Mendicants, meditate in retreat.
For a mendicant who meditates in retreat, things become truly clear.”

16. The End of Relishing
With Koṭṭhita on Impermanence

segs.p: Atha kho āyasmā mahākoṭṭhiko yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami …pe… ekamantaṁ nisinno kho āyasmā koṭṭhiko bhagavantaṁ etadavoca:
segs.e: Then Venerable Mahākoṭṭhita went up to the Buddha … and asked him,

segs.p: “sādhu me, bhante, bhagavā saṅkhittena dhammaṁ desetu, yamahaṁ bhagavato dhammaṁ sutvā eko vūpakaṭṭho appamatto ātāpī pahitatto vihareyyan”ti.
segs.e: “Sir, may the Buddha please teach me Dhamma in brief. When I’ve heard it, I’ll live alone, withdrawn, diligent, keen, and resolute.”

segs.p: “Yaṁ kho, koṭṭhika, aniccaṁ tatra te chando pahātabbo.
segs.e: “Koṭṭhita, you should give up desire for what is impermanent.
And what is impermanent?

segs.p: Cakkhu kho, koṭṭhika, aniccaṁ; tatra te chando pahātabbo.
segs.e: The eye,

segs.p: Rūpā aniccā; tatra te chando pahātabbo.
segs.e: sights,

segs.p: Cakkhuviññāṇaṁ aniccaṁ; tatra te chando pahātabbo.
segs.e: eye consciousness,

segs.p: Cakkhusamphasso anicco; tatra te chando pahātabbo.
segs.e: and eye contact are impermanent: you should give up desire for them.

segs.p: Yampidaṁ cakkhusamphassapaccayā uppajjati vedayitaṁ sukhaṁ vā dukkhaṁ vā adukkhamasukhaṁ vā tampi aniccaṁ; tatra te chando pahātabbo …pe…
segs.e: The pleasant, painful, or neutral feeling that arises dependent on eye contact is also impermanent: you should give up desire for it.

segs.p: jivhā aniccā; tatra te chando pahātabbo.
segs.e: The ear … nose … tongue … body ….

segs.p: Rasā aniccā; tatra te chando pahātabbo.
Jivhāviññāṇaṁ aniccaṁ; tatra te chando pahātabbo.
Jivhāsamphasso anicco; tatra te chando pahātabbo.
Yampidaṁ jivhāsamphassapaccayā uppajjati vedayitaṁ sukhaṁ vā dukkhaṁ vā adukkhamasukhaṁ vā tampi aniccaṁ; tatra te chando pahātabbo …pe…
mano anicco; tatra te chando pahātabbo.
segs.e: The mind,

segs.p: Dhammā aniccā; tatra te chando pahātabbo.
segs.e: ideas,

segs.p: Manoviññāṇaṁ aniccaṁ; tatra te chando pahātabbo.
segs.e: mind consciousness,

segs.p: Manosamphasso anicco; tatra te chando pahātabbo.
segs.e: and mind contact are impermanent: you should give up desire for them.

segs.p: Yampidaṁ manosamphassapaccayā uppajjati vedayitaṁ sukhaṁ vā dukkhaṁ vā adukkhamasukhaṁ vā tampi aniccaṁ; tatra te chando pahātabbo.
segs.e: The pleasant, painful, or neutral feeling that arises dependent on mind contact is also impermanent: you should give up desire for it.

segs.p: Yaṁ kho, koṭṭhika, aniccaṁ tatra te chando pahātabbo”ti.
segs.e: Koṭṭhita, you should give up desire for what is impermanent.”

With Koṭṭhita on Suffering

segs.p: Atha kho āyasmā mahākoṭṭhiko …pe… bhagavantaṁ etadavoca:

segs.e: The pleasant, painful, or neutral feeling that arises dependent on eye contact is also suffering; you should give up desire for it.

segs.p: jivhā dukkhā; tatra te chando pahātabbo …pe…
segs.e: The ear … nose … tongue … body ….

segs.p: mano dukkho; tatra te chando pahātabbo.
segs.e: The mind,

segs.p: Dhammā dukkhā; tatra te chando pahātabbo.
segs.e: ideas,

segs.e: mind consciousness,

segs.e: and mind contact are suffering: you should give up desire for them.

segs.e: The pleasant, painful, or neutral feeling that arises dependent on mind contact is also suffering: you should give up desire for it.

segs.p: Yaṁ kho, koṭṭhika, dukkhaṁ tatra te chando pahātabbo”ti.
segs.e: Koṭṭhita, you should give up desire for what is suffering.”

16. The End of Relishing
With Koṭṭhita on Not-Self

segs.p: “Yo kho, koṭṭhika, anattā tatra te chando pahātabbo.
segs.e: “Koṭṭhita, you should give up desire for what is not-self.
And what is not-self?

segs.p: Cakkhu kho, koṭṭhika, anattā; tatra te chando pahātabbo.
segs.e: The eye,

segs.p: Rūpā anattā; tatra te chando pahātabbo.
segs.e: sights,

segs.p: Cakkhuviññāṇaṁ anattā; tatra te chando pahātabbo.
segs.e: eye consciousness,

segs.p: Cakkhusamphasso anattā; tatra te chando pahātabbo.
segs.e: and eye contact are not-self: you should give up desire for them.

segs.p: Yampidaṁ cakkhusamphassapaccayā uppajjati vedayitaṁ sukhaṁ vā dukkhaṁ vā adukkhamasukhaṁ vā tampi anattā; tatra te chando pahātabbo …pe…
segs.e: The pleasant, painful, or neutral feeling that arises dependent on eye contact is also not-self: You should give up desire for it.

segs.p: jivhā anattā; tatra te chando pahātabbo …pe…
segs.e: The ear … nose … tongue … body …

segs.p: mano anattā; tatra te chando pahātabbo.
segs.e: The mind,

segs.p: Dhammā anattā; tatra te chando pahātabbo.
segs.e: ideas,
mind consciousness,
and mind contact …

segs.p: yampidaṁ manosamphassapaccayā uppajjati vedayitaṁ sukhaṁ vā dukkhaṁ vā adukkhamasukhaṁ vā tampi anattā; tatra te chando pahātabbo.
segs.e: The pleasant, painful, or neutral feeling that arises dependent on mind contact is also not-self: you should give up desire for it.

segs.p: Yo kho, koṭṭhika, anattā, tatra te chando pahātabbo”ti.
segs.e: Koṭṭhita, you should give up desire for what is not-self.”

16. The End of Relishing
Giving Up Wrong View

segs.p: Atha kho aññataro bhikkhu yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami …pe…
segs.e: Then a mendicant went up to the Buddha …

segs.p: ekamantaṁ nisinno so bhikkhu bhagavantaṁ etadavoca:
segs.e: and said to him:

segs.p: “kathaṁ nu kho, bhante, jānato kathaṁ passato micchādiṭṭhi pahīyatī”ti?
segs.e: “Sir, how does one know and see so that wrong view is given up?”

segs.p: “Cakkhuṁ kho, bhikkhu, aniccato jānato passato micchādiṭṭhi pahīyati.
segs.e: “Mendicant, knowing and seeing the eye, sights, eye consciousness, and eye contact as impermanent, wrong view is given up. …

segs.p: Rūpe aniccato jānato passato micchādiṭṭhi pahīyati.
Cakkhuviññāṇaṁ aniccato jānato passato micchādiṭṭhi pahīyati.
Cakkhusamphassaṁ aniccato jānato passato micchādiṭṭhi pahīyati …pe…
yampidaṁ manosamphassapaccayā uppajjati vedayitaṁ sukhaṁ vā dukkhaṁ vā adukkhamasukhaṁ vā tampi aniccato jānato passato micchādiṭṭhi pahīyati.
segs.e: And also knowing and seeing the pleasant, painful, or neutral feeling that arises dependent on mind contact as impermanent, wrong view is given up.

segs.p: Evaṁ kho, bhikkhu, jānato evaṁ passato micchādiṭṭhi pahīyatī”ti.
segs.e: This is how to know and see so that wrong view is given up.”

16. The End of Relishing
Giving Up Substantialist View
Then a mendicant went up to the Buddha …

segs.p: “kathaṁ nu kho, bhante, jānato kathaṁ passato sakkāyadiṭṭhi pahīyatī”ti?

segs.p: “Cakkhuṁ kho, bhikkhu, dukkhato jānato passato sakkāyadiṭṭhi pahīyati.
segs.e: “Mendicant, knowing and seeing the eye, sights, eye consciousness, and eye contact as suffering, substantialist view is given up. …

segs.p: Rūpe dukkhato jānato passato sakkāyadiṭṭhi pahīyati.

segs.e: And also knowing and seeing the pleasant, painful, or neutral feeling that arises dependent on mind contact as suffering, substantialist view is given up.

segs.p: Evaṁ kho, bhikkhu, jānato evaṁ passato sakkāyadiṭṭhi pahīyatī”ti.
segs.e: This is how to know and see so that substantialist view is given up.”

17. Sixty Abbreviated Texts
The Interior Was Impermanent in the Past

segs.p: “Cakkhu, bhikkhave, aniccaṁ atītaṁ …pe… jivhā aniccā atītā …pe… mano anicco atīto.
segs.e: “Mendicants, in the past the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind were impermanent.

segs.p: Evaṁ passaṁ, bhikkhave, sutavā ariyasāvako cakkhusmimpi nibbindati …pe… jivhāyapi nibbindati …pe… manasmimpi nibbindati.
segs.e: Seeing this, a learned noble disciple grows disillusioned with the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.

segs.p: Nibbindaṁ virajjati; virāgā vimuccati; vimuttasmiṁ vimuttamiti ñāṇaṁ hoti.
segs.e: Being disillusioned, desire fades away. When desire fades away they’re freed. When they’re freed, they know they’re freed.

segs.p: ‘Khīṇā jāti, vusitaṁ brahmacariyaṁ, kataṁ karaṇīyaṁ, nāparaṁ itthattāyā’ti pajānātī”ti.
segs.e: They understand: ‘Rebirth is ended, the spiritual journey has been completed, what had to be done has been done, there is nothing further for this place.’”

18. The Ocean
The Ocean (1st)
“Mendicants, an unlearned ordinary person speaks of the ocean.
But that’s not the ocean in the training of the Noble One.
That’s just a large body of water, a large sea of water.
For a person, the eye is an ocean,
and its currents are made of sights.

segs.p: Yo taṁ rūpamayaṁ vegaṁ sahati, ayaṁ vuccati, bhikkhave, atari cakkhusamuddaṁ saūmiṁ sāvaṭṭaṁ sagāhaṁ sarakkhasaṁ;
segs.e: Someone who can prevail over those currents is said to have crossed over the ocean of the eye, with its waves and whirlpools, its saltwater crocodiles and monsters.
Crossed over, gone to the far shore, the brahmin stands on solid ground.
For a person, the ear … nose … tongue … body …

segs.p: Yo taṁ rasamayaṁ vegaṁ sahati, ayaṁ vuccati, bhikkhave, atari jivhāsamuddaṁ saūmiṁ sāvaṭṭaṁ sagāhaṁ sarakkhasaṁ;

segs.e: mind is an ocean,
and its currents are made of ideas.

segs.p: Yo taṁ dhammamayaṁ vegaṁ sahati, ayaṁ vuccati, bhikkhave, atari manosamuddaṁ saūmiṁ sāvaṭṭaṁ sagāhaṁ sarakkhasaṁ;
segs.e: Someone who can prevail over those currents is said to have crossed over the ocean of the mind, with its waves and whirlpools, its saltwater crocodiles and monsters.
Crossed over, gone to the far shore, the brahmin stands on solid ground.”
That is what the Buddha said.
Then the Holy One, the Teacher, went on to say:
“A knowledge master who’s crossed <j>the ocean so hard to cross,
with its saltwater crocodiles and monsters, <j>its waves, whirlpools, and dangers;
they’ve completed the spiritual journey and gone to the end of the world,
they’re called ‘one who has gone beyond’.”
Linked Discourses 35.229
18. The Ocean
The Ocean (2nd)
“Mendicants, an unlearned ordinary person speaks of the ocean.
But that’s not the ocean in the training of the Noble One.
That’s just a large body of water, a large sea of water.

segs.p: Santi, bhikkhave, cakkhuviññeyyā rūpā iṭṭhā kantā manāpā piyarūpā kāmūpasaṁhitā rajanīyā.
segs.e: There are sights known by the eye, which are likable, desirable, agreeable, pleasant, sensual, and arousing.

segs.p: Ayaṁ vuccati, bhikkhave, ariyassa vinaye samuddo.
segs.e: This is called the ocean in the training of the Noble One.

segs.p: Etthāyaṁ sadevako loko samārako sabrahmako sassamaṇabrāhmaṇī pajā sadevamanussā yebhuyyena samunnā tantākulakajātā kulagaṇṭhikajātā muñjapabbajabhūtā, apāyaṁ duggatiṁ vinipātaṁ saṁsāraṁ nātivattati …pe….
segs.e: And it’s here that this world—with its gods, Māras, and divinities, this population with its ascetics and brahmins, gods and humans—is for the most part sunk. It’s become tangled like string, knotted like a ball of thread, and matted like rushes and reeds, and it doesn’t escape the places of loss, the bad places, the underworld, transmigration.

segs.p: Santi, bhikkhave, jivhāviññeyyā rasā …pe… santi, bhikkhave, manoviññeyyā dhammā iṭṭhā kantā manāpā piyarūpā kāmūpasaṁhitā rajanīyā.
segs.e: There are sounds … smells … tastes … touches … ideas known by the mind, which are likable, desirable, agreeable, pleasant, sensual, and arousing.

segs.p: Ayaṁ vuccati, bhikkhave, ariyassa vinaye samuddo.
segs.e: This is called the ocean in the training of the Noble One.

segs.p: Etthāyaṁ sadevako loko samārako sabrahmako sassamaṇabrāhmaṇī pajā sadevamanussā yebhuyyena samunnā tantākulakajātā kulagaṇṭhikajātā muñjapabbajabhūtā apāyaṁ duggatiṁ vinipātaṁ saṁsāraṁ nātivattatīti.
segs.e: And it’s here that this world—with its gods, Māras, and divinities, this population with its ascetics and brahmins, gods and humans—is for the most part sunk. It’s become tangled like string, knotted like a ball of thread, and matted like rushes and reeds, and it doesn’t escape the places of loss, the bad places, the underworld, transmigration.
Those in whom greed, hate, and ignorance
have faded away;
have crossed the ocean so hard to cross,
with its saltwater crocodiles and monsters, <j>its waves and dangers.
They’ve slipped their chains, given up death, and have no attachments.
They’ve given up suffering, <j>so there are no more future lives.
They’ve disappeared, and cannot be measured;
and they’ve confounded the King of Death, I say.”
Linked Discourses 35.230
18. The Ocean
The Simile of the Angler

segs.p: “Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, bāḷisiko āmisagatabaḷisaṁ gambhīre udakarahade pakkhipeyya.
segs.e: “Mendicants, suppose an angler was to cast a baited hook into a deep lake.
Seeing the bait, a fish would swallow it.

segs.p: Evañhi so, bhikkhave, maccho gilitabaḷiso bāḷisikassa anayaṁ āpanno byasanaṁ āpanno yathākāmakaraṇīyo bāḷisikassa.
segs.e: And so the fish that swallowed the hook would meet with tragedy and disaster, and the angler can do what he wants with it.

segs.p: Evameva kho, bhikkhave, chayime baḷisā lokasmiṁ anayāya sattānaṁ vadhāya pāṇinaṁ.
segs.e: In the same way, there are these six hooks in the world that mean tragedy and slaughter for living creatures.
What six?

segs.p: Santi, bhikkhave, cakkhuviññeyyā rūpā iṭṭhā kantā manāpā piyarūpā kāmūpasaṁhitā rajanīyā.
segs.e: There are sights known by the eye, which are likable, desirable, agreeable, pleasant, sensual, and arousing.

segs.p: Tañce bhikkhu abhinandati abhivadati ajjhosāya tiṭṭhati.
segs.e: If a mendicant approves, welcomes, and keeps clinging to them,

segs.p: Ayaṁ vuccati, bhikkhave, bhikkhu gilitabaḷiso, mārassa anayaṁ āpanno byasanaṁ āpanno yathākāmakaraṇīyo pāpimato …pe…
segs.e: they’re called a mendicant who has swallowed Māra’s hook. They’ve met with tragedy and disaster, and the Wicked One can do with them what he wants.
There are sounds … smells … tastes … touches …

segs.p: Santi, bhikkhave, manoviññeyyā dhammā iṭṭhā kantā manāpā piyarūpā kāmūpasaṁhitā rajanīyā.
segs.e: ideas known by the mind, which are likable, desirable, agreeable, pleasant, sensual, and arousing.

segs.p: Tañce bhikkhu abhinandati abhivadati ajjhosāya tiṭṭhati.
segs.e: If a mendicant approves, welcomes, and keeps clinging to them,

segs.p: Ayaṁ vuccati, bhikkhave, bhikkhu gilitabaḷiso mārassa anayaṁ āpanno byasanaṁ āpanno yathākāmakaraṇīyo pāpimato.
segs.e: they’re called a mendicant who has swallowed Māra’s hook. They’ve met with tragedy and disaster, and the Wicked One can do with them what he wants.

segs.p: Santi ca, bhikkhave, cakkhuviññeyyā rūpā iṭṭhā kantā manāpā piyarūpā kāmūpasaṁhitā rajanīyā.
segs.e: There are sights known by the eye, which are likable, desirable, agreeable, pleasant, sensual, and arousing.

segs.p: Tañce, bhikkhu, nābhinandati nābhivadati nājjhosāya tiṭṭhati. Ayaṁ vuccati, bhikkhave, bhikkhu na gilitabaḷiso mārassa abhedi baḷisaṁ paribhedi baḷisaṁ na anayaṁ āpanno na byasanaṁ āpanno na yathākāmakaraṇīyo pāpimato …pe….
segs.e: If a mendicant doesn’t approve, welcome, and keep clinging to them, they’re called a mendicant who hasn’t swallowed Māra’s hook. They’ve broken the hook, destroyed it. They haven’t met with tragedy and disaster, and the Wicked One cannot do with them what he wants.
There are sounds … smells … tastes … touches …

segs.p: Santi, bhikkhave, manoviññeyyā dhammā iṭṭhā kantā manāpā piyarūpā kāmūpasaṁhitā rajanīyā.
segs.e: ideas known by the mind, which are likable, desirable, agreeable, pleasant, sensual, and arousing.

segs.p: Tañce bhikkhu nābhinandati nābhivadati nājjhosāya tiṭṭhati, ayaṁ vuccati, bhikkhave, bhikkhu na gilitabaḷiso mārassa abhedi baḷisaṁ paribhedi baḷisaṁ na anayaṁ āpanno na byasanaṁ āpanno na yathākāmakaraṇīyo pāpimato”ti.
segs.e: If a mendicant doesn’t approve, welcome, and keep clinging to them, they’re called a mendicant who hasn’t swallowed Māra’s hook. They’ve broken the hook, destroyed it. They haven’t met with tragedy and disaster, and the Wicked One cannot do with them what he wants.”

18. The Ocean
The Simile of the Latex-Producing Tree

segs.p: “Yassa kassaci, bhikkhave, bhikkhussa vā bhikkhuniyā vā cakkhuviññeyyesu rūpesu yo rāgo so atthi, yo doso so atthi, yo moho so atthi, yo rāgo so appahīno, yo doso so appahīno, yo moho so appahīno tassa parittā cepi cakkhuviññeyyā rūpā cakkhussa āpāthaṁ āgacchanti pariyādiyantevassa cittaṁ; ko pana vādo adhimattānaṁ.
segs.e: “Mendicants, take any monk or nun who, when it comes to sights known by the eye, still has greed, hate, and delusion, and has not given them up. If even trivial sights come into their range of vision they overcome their mind, let alone those that are compelling.
Why is that?

segs.p: Yo, bhikkhave, rāgo, so atthi, yo doso so atthi, yo moho so atthi, yo rāgo so appahīno, yo doso so appahīno, yo moho so appahīno …pe….
segs.e: Because they still have greed, hate, and delusion, and have not given them up.

segs.p: Yassa kassaci, bhikkhave, bhikkhussa vā bhikkhuniyā vā jivhāviññeyyesu rasesu yo rāgo so atthi …pe….
segs.e: When it comes to sounds … smells … tastes … touches …

segs.p: Yassa kassaci, bhikkhave, bhikkhussa vā bhikkhuniyā vā manoviññeyyesu dhammesu yo rāgo so atthi, yo doso so atthi, yo moho so atthi, yo rāgo so appahīno, yo doso so appahīno, yo moho so appahīno, tassa parittā cepi manoviññeyyā dhammā manassa āpāthaṁ āgacchanti pariyādiyantevassa cittaṁ; ko pana vādo adhimattānaṁ.
segs.e: ideas known by the mind, they still have greed, hate, and delusion, and have not given them up. If even trivial thoughts come into the range of the mind they overcome their mind, let alone those that are compelling.
Why is that?

segs.p: Yo, bhikkhave, rāgo, so atthi, yo doso so atthi, yo moho so atthi, yo rāgo so appahīno, yo doso so appahīno, yo moho so appahīno.
segs.e: Because they still have greed, hate, and delusion, and have not given them up.

segs.p: Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, khīrarukkho assattho vā nigrodho vā pilakkho vā udumbaro vā daharo taruṇo komārako.
segs.e: Suppose there was a latex-producing tree—such as a peepal, a banyan, a wavy leaf fig, or a cluster fig—that’s a tender young sapling.

segs.p: Tamenaṁ puriso tiṇhāya kuṭhāriyā yato yato ābhindeyya āgaccheyya khīran”ti?
segs.e: If a man were to chop it here and there with a sharp axe, would latex come out?”
“Yes, sir.
Why is that?
Because it still has latex.”

segs.p: “Evameva kho, bhikkhave, yassa kassaci bhikkhussa vā bhikkhuniyā vā cakkhuviññeyyesu rūpesu yo rāgo so atthi, yo doso so atthi, yo moho so atthi, yo rāgo so appahīno, yo doso so appahīno, yo moho so appahīno, tassa parittā cepi cakkhuviññeyyā rūpā cakkhussa āpāthaṁ āgacchanti pariyādiyantevassa cittaṁ; ko pana vādo adhimattānaṁ.
segs.e: “In the same way, take any monk or nun who, when it comes to sights known by the eye, still has greed, hate, and delusion, and has not given them up. If even trivial sights come into their range of vision they overcome their mind, let alone those that are compelling.
Why is that?

segs.p: Yo, bhikkhave, rāgo so atthi, yo doso so atthi, yo moho so atthi, yo rāgo so appahīno, yo doso so appahīno, yo moho so appahīno …pe….
segs.e: Because they still have greed, hate, and delusion, and have not given them up.

segs.p: Yassa kassaci, bhikkhave, bhikkhussa vā bhikkhuniyā vā jivhāviññeyyesu rasesu yo rāgo so atthi …pe….
segs.e: When it comes to sounds … smells … tastes … touches …

segs.p: Yassa kassaci, bhikkhave, bhikkhussa vā bhikkhuniyā vā manoviññeyyesu dhammesu yo rāgo so atthi, yo doso so atthi, yo moho so atthi, yo rāgo so appahīno, yo doso so appahīno, yo moho so appahīno, tassa parittā cepi manoviññeyyā dhammā manassa āpāthaṁ āgacchanti pariyādiyantevassa cittaṁ; ko pana vādo adhimattānaṁ.
segs.e: ideas known by the mind, they still have greed, hate, and delusion, and have not given them up. If even trivial thoughts come into the range of the mind they overcome their mind, let alone those that are compelling.
Why is that?

segs.p: Yo, bhikkhave, rāgo so atthi, yo doso so atthi, yo moho so atthi, yo rāgo so appahīno, yo doso so appahīno, yo moho so appahīno.
segs.e: Because they still have greed, hate, and delusion, and have not given them up.

segs.p: Yassa kassaci, bhikkhave, bhikkhussa vā bhikkhuniyā vā cakkhuviññeyyesu rūpesu yo rāgo so natthi, yo doso so natthi, yo moho so natthi, yo rāgo so pahīno, yo doso so pahīno, yo moho so pahīno, tassa adhimattā cepi cakkhuviññeyyā rūpā cakkhussa āpāthaṁ āgacchanti nevassa cittaṁ pariyādiyanti; ko pana vādo parittānaṁ.
segs.e: Take any monk or nun who, when it comes to sights known by the eye, has no greed, hate, and delusion left, and has given them up. If even compelling sights come into their range of vision they don’t overcome their mind, let alone those that are trivial.
Why is that?

segs.p: Yo, bhikkhave, rāgo so natthi, yo doso so natthi, yo moho so natthi, yo rāgo so pahīno, yo doso so pahīno, yo moho so pahīno …pe….
segs.e: Because they have no greed, hate, and delusion left, and have given them up.

segs.p: Yassa kassaci, bhikkhave, bhikkhussa vā bhikkhuniyā vā jivhāviññeyyesu rasesu …pe… manoviññeyyesu dhammesu yo rāgo so natthi, yo doso so natthi, yo moho so natthi, yo rāgo so pahīno, yo doso so pahīno, yo moho so pahīno, tassa adhimattā cepi manoviññeyyā dhammā manassa āpāthaṁ āgacchanti nevassa cittaṁ pariyādiyanti; ko pana vādo parittānaṁ.
segs.e: When it comes to sounds … smells … tastes … touches … ideas known by the mind, they have no greed, hate, and delusion left, and have given them up. If even compelling ideas come into the range of the mind they don’t overcome their mind, let alone those that are trivial.
Why is that?

segs.p: Yo, bhikkhave, rāgo so natthi, yo doso so natthi, yo moho so natthi, yo rāgo so pahīno, yo doso so pahīno, yo moho so pahīno.
segs.e: Because they have no greed, hate, and delusion left, and have given them up.

segs.p: Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, khīrarukkho assattho vā nigrodho vā pilakkho vā udumbaro vā sukkho kolāpo terovassiko.
segs.e: Suppose there was a latex-producing tree—such as a peepal, a banyan, a wavy leaf fig, or a cluster fig—that’s dried up, withered, and decrepit.

segs.p: Tamenaṁ puriso tiṇhāya kuṭhāriyā yato yato ābhindeyya āgaccheyya khīran”ti?
segs.e: If a man were to chop it here and there with a sharp axe, would latex come out?”
“No, sir.
Why is that?
Because it has no latex left.”

segs.p: “Evameva kho, bhikkhave, yassa kassaci bhikkhussa vā bhikkhuniyā vā cakkhuviññeyyesu rūpesu yo rāgo so natthi, yo doso so natthi, yo moho so natthi, yo rāgo so pahīno, yo doso so pahīno, yo moho so pahīno, tassa adhimattā cepi cakkhuviññeyyā rūpā cakkhussa āpāthaṁ āgacchanti nevassa cittaṁ pariyādiyanti; ko pana vādo parittānaṁ.
segs.e: “In the same way, take any monk or nun who, when it comes to sights known by the eye, has no greed, hate, and delusion left, and has given them up. If even compelling sights come into their range of vision they don’t overcome their mind, let alone those that are trivial.
Why is that?

segs.p: Yo, bhikkhave, rāgo so natthi, yo doso so natthi, yo moho so natthi, yo rāgo so pahīno, yo doso so pahīno, yo moho so pahīno …pe….
segs.e: Because they have no greed, hate, and delusion left, and have given them up.

segs.p: Yassa kassaci, bhikkhave, bhikkhussa vā bhikkhuniyā vā jivhāviññeyyesu rasesu …pe….
segs.e: When it comes to sounds … smells … tastes … touches …

segs.p: Yassa kassaci, bhikkhave, bhikkhussa vā bhikkhuniyā vā manoviññeyyesu dhammesu yo rāgo so natthi, yo doso so natthi, yo moho so natthi, yo rāgo so pahīno, yo doso so pahīno, yo moho so pahīno, tassa adhimattā cepi manoviññeyyā dhammā manassa āpāthaṁ āgacchanti, nevassa cittaṁ pariyādiyanti; ko pana vādo parittānaṁ.
segs.e: ideas known by the mind, they have no greed, hate, and delusion left, and have given them up. If even compelling thoughts come into the range of the mind they don’t overcome their mind, let alone those that are trivial.
Why is that?

segs.p: Yo, bhikkhave, rāgo so natthi, yo doso so natthi, yo moho so natthi, yo rāgo so pahīno, yo doso so pahīno, yo moho so pahīno”ti.
segs.e: Because they have no greed, hate, and delusion left, and have given them up.”
Linked Discourses 35.232
18. The Ocean
With Koṭṭhita

segs.p: Ekaṁ samayaṁ āyasmā ca sāriputto āyasmā ca mahākoṭṭhiko bārāṇasiyaṁ viharanti isipatane migadāye.
segs.e: At one time Venerable Sāriputta and Venerable Mahākoṭṭhita were staying near Varanasi in the deer park at Isipatana.

segs.p: Atha kho āyasmā mahākoṭṭhiko sāyanhasamayaṁ paṭisallānā vuṭṭhito yenāyasmā sāriputto tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā āyasmatā sāriputtena saddhiṁ sammodi.
segs.e: Then in the late afternoon, Venerable Mahākoṭṭhita came out of retreat, went to Venerable Sāriputta, and exchanged greetings with him.

segs.p: Sammodanīyaṁ kathaṁ sāraṇīyaṁ vītisāretvā ekamantaṁ nisīdi. Ekamantaṁ nisinno kho āyasmā mahākoṭṭhiko āyasmantaṁ sāriputtaṁ etadavoca:
segs.e: When the greetings and polite conversation were over, he sat down to one side and said to Sāriputta:

segs.p: “Kiṁ nu kho, āvuso sāriputta, cakkhu rūpānaṁ saṁyojanaṁ, rūpā cakkhussa saṁyojanaṁ …pe…
segs.e: “Reverend Sāriputta, which is it? Is the eye the fetter of sights, or are sights the fetter of the eye?

segs.p: jivhā rasānaṁ saṁyojanaṁ, rasā jivhāya saṁyojanaṁ …pe…
segs.e: Is the ear … nose … tongue … body …

segs.p: mano dhammānaṁ saṁyojanaṁ, dhammā manassa saṁyojanan”ti?
segs.e: mind the fetter of ideas, or are ideas the fetter of the mind?”

segs.p: “Na kho, āvuso koṭṭhika, cakkhu rūpānaṁ saṁyojanaṁ, na rūpā cakkhussa saṁyojanaṁ.
segs.e: “Reverend Koṭṭhita, the eye is not the fetter of sights, nor are sights the fetter of the eye.

segs.p: Yañca tattha tadubhayaṁ paṭicca uppajjati chandarāgo taṁ tattha saṁyojanaṁ …pe…
segs.e: The fetter there is the desire and greed that arises from the pair of them.

segs.p: na jivhā rasānaṁ saṁyojanaṁ, na rasā jivhāya saṁyojanaṁ.
segs.e: The ear … nose … tongue … body …

segs.p: Yañca tattha tadubhayaṁ paṭicca uppajjati chandarāgo taṁ tattha saṁyojanaṁ …pe…
na mano dhammānaṁ saṁyojanaṁ, na dhammā manassa saṁyojanaṁ.
segs.e: mind is not the fetter of ideas, nor are ideas the fetter of the mind.

segs.p: Yañca tattha tadubhayaṁ paṭicca uppajjati chandarāgo taṁ tattha saṁyojanaṁ.
segs.e: The fetter there is the desire and greed that arises from the pair of them.

segs.p: Seyyathāpi, āvuso, kāḷo ca balībaddo odāto ca balībaddo ekena dāmena vā yottena vā saṁyuttā assu.
segs.e: Suppose there was a black ox and a white ox yoked by a single harness or yoke.
Would it be right to say that

segs.p: ‘kāḷo balībaddo odātassa balībaddassa saṁyojanaṁ, odāto balībaddo kāḷassa balībaddassa saṁyojanan’ti, sammā nu kho so vadamāno vadeyyā”ti?
segs.e: the black ox is the yoke of the white ox, or the white ox is the yoke of the black ox?”
“No, reverend.

segs.p: “Na kho, āvuso, kāḷo balībaddo odātassa balībaddassa saṁyojanaṁ, na odāto balībaddo kāḷassa balībaddassa saṁyojanaṁ.
segs.e: The black ox is not the yoke of the white ox, nor is the white ox the yoke of the black ox.

segs.p: Yena ca kho te ekena dāmena vā yottena vā saṁyuttā taṁ tattha saṁyojanaṁ.
segs.e: The yoke there is the single harness or yoke that they’re yoked by.”

segs.p: Evameva kho, āvuso, na cakkhu rūpānaṁ saṁyojanaṁ, na rūpā cakkhussa saṁyojanaṁ.
segs.e: “In the same way, the eye is not the fetter of sights, nor are sights the fetter of the eye.

segs.p: Yañca tattha tadubhayaṁ paṭicca uppajjati chandarāgo taṁ tattha saṁyojanaṁ …pe…
segs.e: The fetter there is the desire and greed that arises from the pair of them.
The ear … nose … tongue … body …

segs.p: na mano dhammānaṁ saṁyojanaṁ, na dhammā manassa saṁyojanaṁ.
segs.e: mind is not the fetter of ideas, nor are ideas the fetter of the mind.

segs.p: Yañca tattha tadubhayaṁ paṭicca uppajjati chandarāgo, taṁ tattha saṁyojanaṁ.
segs.e: The fetter there is the desire and greed that arises from the pair of them.

segs.p: Cakkhu vā, āvuso, rūpānaṁ saṁyojanaṁ abhavissa, rūpā vā cakkhussa saṁyojanaṁ, nayidaṁ brahmacariyavāso paññāyetha sammā dukkhakkhayāya.

segs.e: However, since this is not the case, but

segs.e: However, since this is not the case, but

segs.p: yañca tattha tadubhayaṁ paṭicca uppajjati chandarāgo, taṁ tattha saṁyojanaṁ, tasmā brahmacariyavāso paññāyati sammā dukkhakkhayāya.
segs.e: the fetter there is the desire and greed that arises from the pair of them, this living of the spiritual life for the complete ending of suffering is found.

segs.p: Imināpetaṁ, āvuso, pariyāyena veditabbaṁ yathā na cakkhu rūpānaṁ saṁyojanaṁ, na rūpā cakkhussa saṁyojanaṁ.
segs.e: This too is a way to understand how this is so.

segs.p: Yañca tattha tadubhayaṁ paṭicca uppajjati chandarāgo, taṁ tattha saṁyojanaṁ …pe…
na mano dhammānaṁ saṁyojanaṁ, na dhammā manassa saṁyojanaṁ.

segs.e: The Buddha has an eye
with which he sees a sight.
But he has no desire and greed,
for his mind is well freed.
The Buddha has an ear …
nose …
tongue …

But he has no desire and greed,

But he has no desire and greed,

18. The Ocean
With Kāmabhū

segs.p: Ekaṁ samayaṁ āyasmā ca ānando āyasmā ca kāmabhū kosambiyaṁ viharanti ghositārāme.
segs.e: At one time the venerables Ānanda and Kāmabhū were staying near Kosambī in Ghosita’s monastery.

segs.p: Atha kho āyasmā kāmabhū sāyanhasamayaṁ paṭisallānā vuṭṭhito yenāyasmā ānando tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā āyasmatā ānandena saddhiṁ sammodi.
segs.e: Then in the late afternoon, Venerable Kāmabhū came out of retreat, went to Venerable Ānanda, and exchanged greetings with him.

segs.p: Sammodanīyaṁ kathaṁ sāraṇīyaṁ vītisāretvā ekamantaṁ nisīdi. Ekamantaṁ nisinno kho āyasmā kāmabhū āyasmantaṁ ānandaṁ etadavoca:
segs.e: When the greetings and polite conversation were over, he sat down to one side and said to Ānanda:

segs.p: “Kiṁ nu kho, āvuso ānanda, cakkhu rūpānaṁ saṁyojanaṁ, rūpā cakkhussa saṁyojanaṁ …pe…
segs.e: “Reverend Ānanda, which is it? Is the eye the fetter of sights, or are sights the fetter of the eye?

segs.p: jivhā rasānaṁ saṁyojanaṁ, rasā jivhāya saṁyojanaṁ …pe…
segs.e: Is the ear … nose … tongue … body …

segs.p: mano dhammānaṁ saṁyojanaṁ, dhammā manassa saṁyojanan”ti?
segs.e: mind the fetter of ideas, or are ideas the fetter of the mind?”

segs.p: “Na kho, āvuso kāmabhū, cakkhu rūpānaṁ saṁyojanaṁ, na rūpā cakkhussa saṁyojanaṁ.
segs.e: “Reverend Kāmabhū, the eye is not the fetter of sights, nor are sights the fetter of the eye.

segs.p: Yañca tattha tadubhayaṁ paṭicca uppajjati chandarāgo, taṁ tattha saṁyojanaṁ …pe…
segs.e: The fetter there is the desire and greed that arises from the pair of them.

segs.p: na jivhā rasānaṁ saṁyojanaṁ, na rasā jivhāya saṁyojanaṁ …pe…
segs.e: The ear … nose … tongue … body …

segs.p: na mano dhammānaṁ saṁyojanaṁ, na dhammā manassa saṁyojanaṁ.
segs.e: mind is not the fetter of ideas, nor are ideas the fetter of the mind.

segs.p: Yañca tattha tadubhayaṁ paṭicca uppajjati chandarāgo taṁ tattha saṁyojanaṁ.
segs.e: The fetter there is the desire and greed that arises from the pair of them.

segs.p: Seyyathāpi, āvuso, kāḷo ca balībaddo odāto ca balībaddo ekena dāmena vā yottena vā saṁyuttā assu.
segs.e: Suppose there was a black ox and a white ox yoked by a single harness or yoke.
Would it be right to say that

segs.p: ‘kāḷo balībaddo odātassa balībaddassa saṁyojanaṁ, odāto balībaddo kāḷassa balībaddassa saṁyojanan’ti, sammā nu kho so vadamāno vadeyyā”ti?
segs.e: the black ox is the yoke of the white ox, or the white ox is the yoke of the black ox?”
“No, reverend.

segs.p: “Na kho, āvuso, kāḷo balībaddo odātassa balībaddassa saṁyojanaṁ, napi odāto balībaddo kāḷassa balībaddassa saṁyojanaṁ.
segs.e: The black ox is not the yoke of the white ox, nor is the white ox the yoke of the black ox.

segs.p: Yena ca kho te ekena dāmena vā yottena vā saṁyuttā, taṁ tattha saṁyojanaṁ.
segs.e: The yoke there is the single harness or yoke that they’re yoked by.”

segs.p: Evameva kho, āvuso, na cakkhu rūpānaṁ saṁyojanaṁ, na rūpā cakkhussa saṁyojanaṁ …pe…
segs.e: “In the same way, the eye is not the fetter of sights, nor are sights the fetter of the eye.
The ear … nose … tongue … body …
mind is not the fetter of ideas, nor are ideas the fetter of the mind.

segs.p: yañca tattha tadubhayaṁ paṭicca uppajjati chandarāgo, taṁ tattha saṁyojanan”ti.
segs.e: The fetter there is the desire and greed that arises from the pair of them.”

18. The Ocean
With Udāyī

segs.p: Ekaṁ samayaṁ āyasmā ca ānando āyasmā ca udāyī kosambiyaṁ viharanti ghositārāme.
segs.e: At one time the venerables Ānanda and Udāyī were staying near Kosambī in Ghosita’s monastery.

segs.p: Atha kho āyasmā udāyī sāyanhasamayaṁ paṭisallānā vuṭṭhito yenāyasmā ānando tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā āyasmatā ānandena saddhiṁ sammodi.
segs.e: Then in the late afternoon, Venerable Udāyī came out of retreat, went to Venerable Ānanda, and exchanged greetings with him.

segs.p: Sammodanīyaṁ kathaṁ sāraṇīyaṁ vītisāretvā ekamantaṁ nisīdi. Ekamantaṁ nisinno kho āyasmā udāyī āyasmantaṁ ānandaṁ etadavoca:
segs.e: When the greetings and polite conversation were over, he sat down to one side and said to Ānanda:

segs.p: “Yatheva nu kho, āvuso ānanda, ayaṁ kāyo bhagavatā anekapariyāyena akkhāto vivaṭo pakāsito:
segs.e: “Reverend Ānanda, the Buddha has explained, opened, and revealed in many ways how this body is not-self.

segs.p: ‘itipāyaṁ kāyo anattā’ti, sakkā evameva viññāṇaṁ pidaṁ ācikkhituṁ desetuṁ paññapetuṁ paṭṭhapetuṁ vivarituṁ vibhajituṁ uttānīkātuṁ: ‘itipidaṁ viññāṇaṁ anattā’”ti?
segs.e: Is it possible to explain consciousness in the same way? To teach, assert, establish, clarify, analyze, and reveal how consciousness is not-self?”

segs.p: “Yatheva kho, āvuso udāyī, ayaṁ kāyo bhagavatā anekapariyāyena akkhāto vivaṭo pakāsito:
‘itipāyaṁ kāyo anattā’ti, sakkā evameva viññāṇaṁ pidaṁ ācikkhituṁ desetuṁ paññapetuṁ paṭṭhapetuṁ vivarituṁ vibhajituṁ uttānīkātuṁ: ‘itipidaṁ viññāṇaṁ anattā’”ti.
segs.e: “It is possible, Reverend Udāyī.

segs.p: “Cakkhuñca, āvuso, paṭicca rūpe ca uppajjati cakkhuviññāṇan”ti?
segs.e: Does eye consciousness arise dependent on the eye and sights?”
“Yes, reverend.”

segs.p: “Yo cāvuso, hetu, yo ca paccayo cakkhuviññāṇassa uppādāya, so ca hetu, so ca paccayo sabbena sabbaṁ sabbathā sabbaṁ aparisesaṁ nirujjheyya. Api nu kho cakkhuviññāṇaṁ paññāyethā”ti?
segs.e: “If the cause and reason that gives rise to eye consciousness were to totally and utterly cease without remainder, would eye consciousness still be found?”
“No, reverend.”

segs.p: “Imināpi kho etaṁ, āvuso, pariyāyena bhagavatā akkhātaṁ vivaṭaṁ pakāsitaṁ: ‘itipidaṁ viññāṇaṁ anattā’”ti …pe….
segs.e: “In this way, too, it can be understood how consciousness is not-self.
Does ear … nose … tongue … body …

segs.p: “Yo cāvuso, hetu yo ca paccayo jivhāviññāṇassa uppādāya, so ca hetu, so ca paccayo sabbena sabbaṁ sabbathā sabbaṁ aparisesaṁ nirujjheyya, api nu kho jivhāviññāṇaṁ paññāyethā”ti?
“Imināpi kho etaṁ, āvuso, pariyāyena bhagavatā akkhātaṁ vivaṭaṁ pakāsitaṁ: ‘itipidaṁ viññāṇaṁ anattā’”ti …pe….

segs.e: mind consciousness arise dependent on the mind and ideas?”
“Yes, reverend.”

segs.p: “Yo cāvuso, hetu, yo ca paccayo manoviññāṇassa uppādāya, so ca hetu, so ca paccayo sabbena sabbaṁ sabbathā sabbaṁ aparisesaṁ nirujjheyya, api nu kho manoviññāṇaṁ paññāyethā”ti?
segs.e: “If the cause and reason that gives rise to mind consciousness were to totally and utterly cease without remainder, would mind consciousness still be found?”
“No, reverend.”

segs.p: “Imināpi kho etaṁ, āvuso, pariyāyena bhagavatā akkhātaṁ vivaṭaṁ pakāsitaṁ: ‘itipidaṁ viññāṇaṁ anattā’ti.
segs.e: “In this way, too, it can be understood how consciousness is not-self.

segs.p: Seyyathāpi, āvuso, puriso sāratthiko sāragavesī sārapariyesanaṁ caramāno tiṇhaṁ kuṭhāriṁ ādāya vanaṁ paviseyya. So tattha passeyya mahantaṁ kadalikkhandhaṁ ujuṁ navaṁ akukkukajātaṁ. Tamenaṁ mūle chindeyya; mūle chetvā agge chindeyya; agge chetvā pattavaṭṭiṁ vinibbhujeyya. So tattha pheggumpi nādhigaccheyya, kuto sāraṁ.
segs.e: Suppose there was a person in need of heartwood. Wandering in search of heartwood, they’d take a sharp axe and enter a forest. There they’d see a big banana trunk, straight and young and grown unskewed. They’d cut it down at the base, cut off the root, cut off the top, and unroll the coiled sheaths. But they wouldn’t even find sapwood, much less heartwood.

segs.p: Evameva kho, āvuso, bhikkhu chasu phassāyatanesu nevattānaṁ na attaniyaṁ samanupassati.
segs.e: In the same way, a mendicant sees these six fields of contact as neither self nor belonging to self.

segs.p: So evaṁ asamanupassanto na kiñci loke upādiyati.
segs.e: So seeing, they don’t grasp anything in the world.

segs.p: Anupādiyaṁ na paritassati. Aparitassaṁ paccattaññeva parinibbāyati.
segs.e: Not grasping, they’re not anxious. Not being anxious, they personally become extinguished.

segs.p: ‘Khīṇā jāti, vusitaṁ brahmacariyaṁ, kataṁ karaṇīyaṁ, nāparaṁ itthattāyā’ti pajānātī”ti.
segs.e: They understand: ‘Rebirth is ended, the spiritual journey has been completed, what had to be done has been done, there is nothing further for this place.’”

18. The Ocean
The Exposition on Burning
“Mendicants, I will teach you an exposition of the teaching on burning.
Listen …
And what is the exposition of the teaching on burning?

segs.p: Varaṁ, bhikkhave, tattāya ayosalākāya ādittāya sampajjalitāya sajotibhūtāya cakkhundriyaṁ sampalimaṭṭhaṁ, na tveva cakkhuviññeyyesu rūpesu anubyañjanaso nimittaggāho.
segs.e: You’d be better off mutilating your eye faculty with a red-hot iron nail, burning, blazing, and glowing, than getting caught up in the features by way of the details in sights known by the eye.

segs.p: Nimittassādagathitaṁ vā, bhikkhave, viññāṇaṁ tiṭṭhamānaṁ tiṭṭheyya, anubyañjanassādagathitaṁ vā tasmiñce samaye kālaṁ kareyya, ṭhānametaṁ vijjati, yaṁ dvinnaṁ gatīnaṁ aññataraṁ gatiṁ gaccheyya—
segs.e: Should consciousness tied to gratification in the features or details continue to remain, and you were to die at that time, it’s possible you would go to one of two destinations:
hell or the animal realm.

segs.p: Imaṁ khvāhaṁ, bhikkhave, ādīnavaṁ disvā evaṁ vadāmi.
segs.e: I speak having seen this drawback.

segs.p: Varaṁ, bhikkhave, tiṇhena ayosaṅkunā ādittena sampajjalitena sajotibhūtena sotindriyaṁ sampalimaṭṭhaṁ, na tveva sotaviññeyyesu saddesu anubyañjanaso nimittaggāho.
segs.e: You’d be better off mutilating your ear faculty with a sharp iron spike …

segs.p: Nimittassādagathitaṁ vā, bhikkhave, viññāṇaṁ tiṭṭhamānaṁ tiṭṭheyya, anubyañjanassādagathitaṁ vā tasmiñce samaye kālaṁ kareyya, ṭhānametaṁ vijjati, yaṁ dvinnaṁ gatīnaṁ aññataraṁ gatiṁ gaccheyya—
Imaṁ khvāhaṁ, bhikkhave, ādīnavaṁ disvā evaṁ vadāmi.
Varaṁ, bhikkhave, tiṇhena nakhacchedanena ādittena sampajjalitena sajotibhūtena ghānindriyaṁ sampalimaṭṭhaṁ, na tveva ghānaviññeyyesu gandhesu anubyañjanaso nimittaggāho.
segs.e: You’d be better off mutilating your nose faculty with a sharp nail cutter …

segs.p: Nimittassādagathitaṁ vā, bhikkhave, viññāṇaṁ tiṭṭhamānaṁ tiṭṭheyya, anubyañjanassādagathitaṁ vā tasmiñce samaye kālaṁ kareyya.
Ṭhānametaṁ vijjati, yaṁ dvinnaṁ gatīnaṁ aññataraṁ gatiṁ gaccheyya—
Imaṁ khvāhaṁ, bhikkhave, ādīnavaṁ disvā evaṁ vadāmi.
Varaṁ, bhikkhave, tiṇhena khurena ādittena sampajjalitena sajotibhūtena jivhindriyaṁ sampalimaṭṭhaṁ, na tveva jivhāviññeyyesu rasesu anubyañjanaso nimittaggāho.
segs.e: You’d be better off mutilating your tongue faculty with a sharp razor …

segs.p: Nimittassādagathitaṁ vā, bhikkhave, viññāṇaṁ tiṭṭhamānaṁ tiṭṭheyya, anubyañjanassādagathitaṁ vā tasmiñce samaye kālaṁ kareyya.
Ṭhānametaṁ vijjati, yaṁ dvinnaṁ gatīnaṁ aññataraṁ gatiṁ gaccheyya—
Imaṁ khvāhaṁ, bhikkhave, ādīnavaṁ disvā evaṁ vadāmi.
Varaṁ, bhikkhave, tiṇhāya sattiyā ādittāya sampajjalitāya sajotibhūtāya kāyindriyaṁ sampalimaṭṭhaṁ, na tveva kāyaviññeyyesu phoṭṭhabbesu anubyañjanaso nimittaggāho.
segs.e: You’d be better off mutilating your body faculty with a sharp spear, burning, blazing, and glowing, than getting caught up in the features by way of the details in touches known by the body.

segs.p: Nimittassādagathitaṁ vā, bhikkhave, viññāṇaṁ tiṭṭhamānaṁ tiṭṭheyya, anubyañjanassādagathitaṁ vā tasmiñce samaye kālaṁ kareyya.
segs.e: Should consciousness tied to gratification in the features or details continue to remain, and you were to die at that time, it’s possible you would go to one of two destinations:

segs.p: Ṭhānametaṁ vijjati, yaṁ dvinnaṁ gatīnaṁ aññataraṁ gatiṁ gaccheyya—

segs.e: hell or the animal realm.

segs.p: Imaṁ khvāhaṁ, bhikkhave, ādīnavaṁ disvā evaṁ vadāmi.
segs.e: I speak having seen this drawback.
You’d be better off sleeping.

segs.p: Sottaṁ kho panāhaṁ, bhikkhave, vañjhaṁ jīvitānaṁ vadāmi, aphalaṁ jīvitānaṁ vadāmi, momūhaṁ jīvitānaṁ vadāmi, na tveva tathārūpe vitakke vitakkeyya yathārūpānaṁ vitakkānaṁ vasaṁ gato saṅghaṁ bhindeyya.
segs.e: For I say that sleep is useless, fruitless, and folly for the living. But while you’re asleep you won’t fall under the sway of such thoughts that would make you create a schism in the Saṅgha.

segs.p: Imaṁ khvāhaṁ, bhikkhave, vañjhaṁ jīvitānaṁ ādīnavaṁ disvā evaṁ vadāmi.
segs.e: I speak having seen this drawback.

segs.p: Tattha, bhikkhave, sutavā ariyasāvako iti paṭisañcikkhati:
segs.e: A learned noble disciple reflects on this:

segs.p: ‘tiṭṭhatu tāva tattāya ayosalākāya ādittāya sampajjalitāya sajotibhūtāya cakkhundriyaṁ sampalimaṭṭhaṁ.
segs.e: ‘Forget mutilating the eye faculty with a red-hot iron nail, burning, blazing, and glowing!
I’d better focus on the fact that

segs.p: iti cakkhu aniccaṁ, rūpā aniccā, cakkhuviññāṇaṁ aniccaṁ, cakkhusamphasso anicco, yampidaṁ cakkhusamphassapaccayā uppajjati vedayitaṁ sukhaṁ vā dukkhaṁ vā adukkhamasukhaṁ vā tampi aniccaṁ’.
segs.e: the eye, sights, eye consciousness, and eye contact are impermanent. And the painful, pleasant, or neutral feeling that arises dependent on eye contact is also impermanent.

segs.p: Tiṭṭhatu tāva tiṇhena ayosaṅkunā ādittena sampajjalitena sajotibhūtena sotindriyaṁ sampalimaṭṭhaṁ.
segs.e: Forget mutilating the ear faculty with a sharp iron spike, burning, blazing, and glowing!
I’d better focus on the fact that

segs.p: iti sotaṁ aniccaṁ, saddā aniccā, sotaviññāṇaṁ aniccaṁ, sotasamphasso anicco, yampidaṁ sotasamphassapaccayā uppajjati vedayitaṁ sukhaṁ vā dukkhaṁ vā adukkhamasukhaṁ vā tampi aniccaṁ.
segs.e: the ear, sounds, ear consciousness, and ear contact are impermanent. And the painful, pleasant, or neutral feeling that arises dependent on ear contact is also impermanent.

segs.p: Tiṭṭhatu tāva tiṇhena nakhacchedanena ādittena sampajjalitena sajotibhūtena ghānindriyaṁ sampalimaṭṭhaṁ.
segs.e: Forget mutilating the nose faculty with a sharp nail cutter, burning, blazing, and glowing!
I’d better focus on the fact that

segs.p: iti ghānaṁ aniccaṁ, gandhā aniccā, ghānaviññāṇaṁ aniccaṁ, ghānasamphasso anicco, yampidaṁ ghānasamphassapaccayā uppajjati vedayitaṁ …pe… tampi aniccaṁ.
segs.e: the nose, smells, nose consciousness, and nose contact are impermanent. And the painful, pleasant, or neutral feeling that arises dependent on nose contact is also impermanent.

segs.p: Tiṭṭhatu tāva tiṇhena khurena ādittena sampajjalitena sajotibhūtena jivhindriyaṁ sampalimaṭṭhaṁ.
segs.e: Forget mutilating the tongue faculty with a sharp razor, burning, blazing, and glowing!
I’d better focus on the fact that

segs.p: iti jivhā aniccā, rasā aniccā, jivhāviññāṇaṁ aniccaṁ, jivhāsamphasso anicco, yampidaṁ jivhāsamphassapaccayā uppajjati …pe… tampi aniccaṁ.
segs.e: the tongue, tastes, tongue consciousness, and tongue contact are impermanent. And the painful, pleasant, or neutral feeling that arises dependent on tongue contact is also impermanent.

segs.p: Tiṭṭhatu tāva tiṇhāya sattiyā ādittāya sampajjalitāya sajotibhūtāya kāyindriyaṁ sampalimaṭṭhaṁ.
segs.e: Forget mutilating the body faculty with a sharp spear, burning, blazing, and glowing!
I’d better focus on the fact that

segs.p: iti kāyo anicco, phoṭṭhabbā aniccā, kāyaviññāṇaṁ aniccaṁ, kāyasamphasso anicco, yampidaṁ kāyasamphassapaccayā uppajjati vedayitaṁ …pe… tampi aniccaṁ.
segs.e: the body, touches, body consciousness, and body contact are impermanent. And the painful, pleasant, or neutral feeling that arises dependent on body contact is also impermanent.
Forget sleeping!
I’d better focus on the fact that

segs.p: iti mano anicco, dhammā aniccā, manoviññāṇaṁ aniccaṁ, manosamphasso anicco, yampidaṁ manosamphassapaccayā uppajjati vedayitaṁ sukhaṁ vā dukkhaṁ vā adukkhamasukhaṁ vā tampi aniccaṁ’.
segs.e: the mind, ideas, mind consciousness, and mind contact are impermanent. And the painful, pleasant, or neutral feeling that arises dependent on mind contact is also impermanent.’

segs.p: Evaṁ passaṁ, bhikkhave, sutavā ariyasāvako cakkhusmimpi nibbindati, rūpesupi nibbindati, cakkhuviññāṇepi nibbindati, cakkhusamphassepi nibbindati …pe…
segs.e: Seeing this, a learned noble disciple grows disillusioned with the eye, sights, eye consciousness, and eye contact. And they grow disillusioned with the painful, pleasant, or neutral feeling that arises dependent on eye contact.

segs.p: yampidaṁ manosamphassapaccayā uppajjati vedayitaṁ sukhaṁ vā dukkhaṁ vā adukkhamasukhaṁ vā tasmimpi nibbindati.
segs.e: They grow disillusioned with the ear … nose … tongue … body … mind … painful, pleasant, or neutral feeling that arises dependent on mind contact.

segs.p: Nibbindaṁ virajjati; virāgā vimuccati; vimuttasmiṁ vimuttamiti ñāṇaṁ hoti.
segs.e: Being disillusioned, desire fades away. When desire fades away they’re freed. When they’re freed, they know they’re freed.

segs.p: ‘Khīṇā jāti, vusitaṁ brahmacariyaṁ, kataṁ karaṇīyaṁ, nāparaṁ itthattāyā’ti pajānāti.
segs.e: They understand: ‘Rebirth is ended, the spiritual journey has been completed, what had to be done has been done, there is nothing further for this place.’
This is the exposition of the teaching on burning.”
Linked Discourses 35.236
18. The Ocean
The Simile of Hands and Feet (1st)
“Mendicants, when there are hands, picking up and putting down are found.
When there are feet, coming and going are found.
When there are joints, contracting and extending are found.
When there’s a belly, hunger and thirst are found.

segs.p: Evameva kho, bhikkhave, cakkhusmiṁ sati cakkhusamphassapaccayā uppajjati ajjhattaṁ sukhaṁ dukkhaṁ …pe…
segs.e: In the same way, when there’s an eye, pleasure and pain arise internally conditioned by eye contact.

segs.p: jivhāya sati jivhāsamphassapaccayā uppajjati ajjhattaṁ sukhaṁ dukkhaṁ …pe…
segs.e: When there’s an ear … nose … tongue … body …

segs.p: manasmiṁ sati manosamphassapaccayā uppajjati ajjhattaṁ sukhaṁ dukkhaṁ …pe….
segs.e: mind, pleasure and pain arise internally conditioned by mind contact.

segs.p: Hatthesu, bhikkhave, asati ādānanikkhepanaṁ na paññāyati;
segs.e: When there are no hands, picking up and putting down aren’t found.
When there are no feet, coming and going aren’t found.
When there are no joints, contracting and extending aren’t found.

segs.p: kucchismiṁ asati jighacchā pipāsā na paññāyati.
segs.e: When there’s no belly, hunger and thirst aren’t found.

segs.p: Evameva kho, bhikkhave, cakkhusmiṁ asati cakkhusamphassapaccayā nuppajjati ajjhattaṁ sukhaṁ dukkhaṁ …pe…
segs.e: In the same way, when there’s no eye, pleasure and pain don’t arise internally conditioned by eye contact.
When there’s no ear … nose … tongue … body …

segs.p: manasmiṁ asati manosamphassapaccayā nuppajjati ajjhattaṁ sukhaṁ dukkhan”ti.
segs.e: mind, pleasure and pain don’t arise internally conditioned by mind contact.”
Linked Discourses 35.237
18. The Ocean
The Simile of Hands and Feet (2nd)
“Mendicants, when there are hands, there’s picking up and putting down.
When there are feet, there’s coming and going.
When there are joints, there’s contracting and extending.
When there’s a belly, there’s hunger and thirst.

segs.p: Evameva kho, bhikkhave, cakkhusmiṁ sati cakkhusamphassapaccayā uppajjati ajjhattaṁ sukhaṁ dukkhaṁ …pe…
segs.e: In the same way, when there’s an eye, pleasure and pain arise internally conditioned by eye contact.
When there’s an ear … nose … tongue … body …

segs.p: manasmiṁ sati manosamphassapaccayā uppajjati ajjhattaṁ sukhaṁ dukkhaṁ …pe….
segs.e: mind, pleasure and pain arise internally conditioned by mind contact.

segs.p: Hatthesu, bhikkhave, asati ādānanikkhepanaṁ na hoti;
segs.e: When there are no hands, there’s no picking up and putting down.
When there are no feet, there’s no coming and going.
When there are no joints, there’s no contracting and extending.

segs.p: kucchismiṁ asati jighacchā pipāsā na hoti.
segs.e: When there’s no belly, there’s no hunger and thirst.

segs.p: Evameva kho, bhikkhave, cakkhusmiṁ asati cakkhusamphassapaccayā nuppajjati ajjhattaṁ sukhaṁ dukkhaṁ …pe…
segs.e: In the same way, when there’s no eye, pleasure and pain don’t arise internally conditioned by eye contact.
When there’s no ear … nose … tongue … body …

segs.p: manasmiṁ asati manosamphassapaccayā nuppajjati ajjhattaṁ sukhaṁ dukkhan”ti.
segs.e: mind, pleasure and pain don’t arise internally conditioned by mind contact.”
Linked Discourses 35.238
19. The Simile of the Vipers
The Simile of the Vipers
“Mendicants, suppose there were four venomous vipers of awesome might.

segs.p: Atha puriso āgaccheyya jīvitukāmo amaritukāmo sukhakāmo dukkhappaṭikūlo.
segs.e: Then a person would come along who wants to live and doesn’t want to die, who wants to be happy and recoils from pain.
They’d say to him,

segs.p: ‘ime te, ambho purisa, cattāro āsīvisā uggatejā ghoravisā kālena kālaṁ vuṭṭhāpetabbā, kālena kālaṁ nhāpetabbā, kālena kālaṁ bhojetabbā, kālena kālaṁ saṁvesetabbā.
segs.e: ‘My man, here are four venomous vipers of awesome might. They must be periodically picked up, washed, fed, and put to sleep.

segs.p: Yadā ca kho te, ambho purisa, imesaṁ catunnaṁ āsīvisānaṁ uggatejānaṁ ghoravisānaṁ aññataro vā aññataro vā kuppissati, tato tvaṁ, ambho purisa, maraṇaṁ vā nigacchasi, maraṇamattaṁ vā dukkhaṁ.
segs.e: But when one or other of these four venomous vipers gets angry with you, you’ll meet with death or deadly pain.

segs.p: Yaṁ te, ambho purisa, karaṇīyaṁ taṁ karohī’ti.
segs.e: So then, my man, do what has to be done.’

segs.p: Atha kho so, bhikkhave, puriso bhīto catunnaṁ āsīvisānaṁ uggatejānaṁ ghoravisānaṁ yena vā tena vā palāyetha.
segs.e: Then that man, terrified of those four venomous vipers, would flee this way or that.
They’d say to him,

segs.p: ‘ime kho, ambho purisa, pañca vadhakā paccatthikā piṭṭhito piṭṭhito anubandhā, yattheva naṁ passissāma tattheva jīvitā voropessāmāti.
segs.e: ‘My man, there are five deadly enemies chasing you, thinking: “When we catch sight of him, we’ll murder him right there!”

segs.p: Yaṁ te, ambho purisa, karaṇīyaṁ taṁ karohī’ti.
segs.e: So then, my man, do what has to be done.’

segs.p: Atha kho so, bhikkhave, puriso bhīto catunnaṁ āsīvisānaṁ uggatejānaṁ ghoravisānaṁ, bhīto pañcannaṁ vadhakānaṁ paccatthikānaṁ yena vā tena vā palāyetha.
segs.e: Then that man, terrified of those four venomous vipers and those five deadly enemies, would flee this way or that.
They’d say to him,

segs.p: ‘ayaṁ te, ambho purisa, chaṭṭho antaracaro vadhako ukkhittāsiko piṭṭhito piṭṭhito anubandho yattheva naṁ passissāmi tattheva siro pātessāmīti.
segs.e: ‘My man, there’s a sixth hidden killer chasing you with a drawn sword, thinking: “When I catch sight of him, I’ll chop off his head right there!”

segs.p: Yaṁ te, ambho purisa, karaṇīyaṁ taṁ karohī’ti.
segs.e: So then, my man, do what has to be done.’

segs.p: Atha kho so, bhikkhave, puriso bhīto catunnaṁ āsīvisānaṁ uggatejānaṁ ghoravisānaṁ, bhīto pañcannaṁ vadhakānaṁ paccatthikānaṁ, bhīto chaṭṭhassa antaracarassa vadhakassa ukkhittāsikassa yena vā tena vā palāyetha.
segs.e: Then that man, terrified of those four venomous vipers and those five deadly enemies and the hidden killer, would flee this way or that.
He’d see an empty village.

segs.p: Yaññadeva gharaṁ paviseyya rittakaññeva paviseyya tucchakaññeva paviseyya suññakaññeva paviseyya.
segs.e: But whatever house he enters is vacant, deserted, and empty.

segs.p: Yaññadeva bhājanaṁ parimaseyya rittakaññeva parimaseyya tucchakaññeva parimaseyya suññakaññeva parimaseyya.
segs.e: And whatever vessel he touches is vacant, hollow, and empty.
They’d say to him,

segs.p: ‘idāni, ambho purisa, imaṁ suññaṁ gāmaṁ corā gāmaghātakā pavisanti.
segs.e: ‘My man, there are bandits who raid villages, and they’re striking now.

segs.p: Yaṁ te, ambho purisa, karaṇīyaṁ taṁ karohī’ti.
segs.e: So then, my man, do what has to be done.’

segs.p: Atha kho so, bhikkhave, puriso bhīto catunnaṁ āsīvisānaṁ uggatejānaṁ ghoravisānaṁ, bhīto pañcannaṁ vadhakānaṁ paccatthikānaṁ, bhīto chaṭṭhassa antaracarassa vadhakassa ukkhittāsikassa, bhīto corānaṁ gāmaghātakānaṁ yena vā tena vā palāyetha.
segs.e: Then that man, terrified of those four venomous vipers and those five deadly enemies and the hidden killer and the bandits, would flee this way or that.

segs.p: So passeyya mahantaṁ udakaṇṇavaṁ orimaṁ tīraṁ sāsaṅkaṁ sappaṭibhayaṁ, pārimaṁ tīraṁ khemaṁ appaṭibhayaṁ.
segs.e: He’d see a large deluge, whose near shore is dubious and perilous, while the far shore is a sanctuary free of peril.

segs.p: Na cassa nāvā santāraṇī uttarasetu vā apārā pāraṁ gamanāya.
segs.e: But there’s no ferryboat or bridge for crossing over.

segs.p: Atha kho, bhikkhave, tassa purisassa evamassa:
segs.e: Then that man would think,

segs.p: ‘ayaṁ kho mahāudakaṇṇavo orimaṁ tīraṁ sāsaṅkaṁ sappaṭibhayaṁ, pārimaṁ tīraṁ khemaṁ appaṭibhayaṁ, natthi ca nāvā santāraṇī uttarasetu vā apārā pāraṁ gamanāya.
Yannūnāhaṁ tiṇakaṭṭhasākhāpalāsaṁ saṅkaḍḍhitvā kullaṁ bandhitvā taṁ kullaṁ nissāya hatthehi ca pādehi ca vāyamamāno sotthinā pāraṁ gaccheyyan’ti.
segs.e: ‘Why don’t I gather grass, sticks, branches, and leaves and make a raft? Riding on the raft, and paddling with my hands and feet, I can safely reach the far shore.’

segs.p: Atha kho so, bhikkhave, puriso tiṇakaṭṭhasākhāpalāsaṁ saṅkaḍḍhitvā kullaṁ bandhitvā taṁ kullaṁ nissāya hatthehi ca pādehi ca vāyamamāno sotthinā pāraṁ gaccheyya, tiṇṇo pāraṅgato thale tiṭṭhati brāhmaṇo.
segs.e: And so that man did exactly that. Having crossed over and gone to the far shore, the brahmin stands on solid ground.

segs.p: Upamā kho myāyaṁ, bhikkhave, katā atthassa viññāpanāya.
segs.e: I’ve made up this simile to make a point.
And this is the point.

segs.p: cattāro āsīvisā uggatejā ghoravisāti kho, bhikkhave, catunnetaṁ mahābhūtānaṁ adhivacanaṁ—
segs.e: ‘Four venomous vipers of awesome might’ is a term for the four principal states:
the elements of earth, water, fire, and air.

segs.p: Pañca vadhakā paccatthikāti kho, bhikkhave, pañcannetaṁ upādānakkhandhānaṁ adhivacanaṁ, seyyathidaṁ—
segs.e: ‘Five deadly enemies’ is a term for the five grasping aggregates, that is:
form, feeling, perception, choices, and consciousness.

segs.p: Chaṭṭho antaracaro vadhako ukkhittāsikoti kho, bhikkhave, nandīrāgassetaṁ adhivacanaṁ.
segs.e: ‘The sixth hidden killer with a drawn sword’ is a term for relishing and greed.

segs.p: Suñño gāmoti kho, bhikkhave, channetaṁ ajjhattikānaṁ āyatanānaṁ adhivacanaṁ.
segs.e: ‘Empty village’ is a term for the six interior sense fields.

segs.p: Cakkhuto cepi naṁ, bhikkhave, paṇḍito byatto medhāvī upaparikkhati rittakaññeva khāyati, tucchakaññeva khāyati, suññakaññeva khāyati …pe…
segs.e: If an astute, competent, intelligent person investigates that in relation to the eye, it appears vacant, hollow, and empty.
If an astute, competent, intelligent person investigates that in relation to the ear … nose … tongue … body …

segs.p: manato cepi naṁ, bhikkhave, paṇḍito byatto medhāvī upaparikkhati rittakaññeva khāyati, tucchakaññeva khāyati, suññakaññeva khāyati.
segs.e: mind, it appears vacant, hollow, and empty.

segs.p: Corā gāmaghātakāti kho, bhikkhave, channetaṁ bāhirānaṁ āyatanānaṁ adhivacanaṁ.
segs.e: ‘Bandits who raid villages’ is a term for the six exterior sense fields.
The eye is struck by both agreeable and disagreeable sights.
The ear …
nose …
tongue …
body …
mind is struck by both agreeable and disagreeable ideas.

segs.p: Mahā udakaṇṇavoti kho, bhikkhave, catunnetaṁ oghānaṁ adhivacanaṁ—
segs.e: ‘Large deluge’ is a term for the four floods:
the floods of sensual pleasures, desire to be reborn, views, and ignorance.

segs.p: Orimaṁ tīraṁ sāsaṅkaṁ sappaṭibhayanti kho, bhikkhave, sakkāyassetaṁ adhivacanaṁ.
segs.e: ‘The near shore that’s dubious and perilous’ is a term for substantial reality.

segs.p: Pārimaṁ tīraṁ khemaṁ appaṭibhayanti kho, bhikkhave, nibbānassetaṁ adhivacanaṁ.
segs.e: ‘The far shore, a sanctuary free of peril’ is a term for extinguishment.

segs.p: Kullanti kho, bhikkhave, ariyassetaṁ aṭṭhaṅgikassa maggassa adhivacanaṁ, seyyathidaṁ—
segs.e: ‘The raft’ is a term for the noble eightfold path, that is:
right view, right purpose, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right immersion.

segs.p: Tassa hatthehi ca pādehi ca vāyāmoti kho, bhikkhave, vīriyārambhassetaṁ adhivacanaṁ.
segs.e: ‘Paddling with hands and feet’ is a term for rousing energy.

segs.p: Tiṇṇo pāraṅgato thale tiṭṭhati brāhmaṇoti kho, bhikkhave, arahato etaṁ adhivacanan”ti.
segs.e: ‘Crossed over, gone to the far shore, the brahmin stands on solid ground’ is a term for a perfected one.”
Linked Discourses 35.239
19. The Simile of the Vipers
The Simile of the Chariot

segs.p: “Tīhi, bhikkhave, dhammehi samannāgato bhikkhu diṭṭheva dhamme sukhasomanassabahulo viharati, yoni cassa āraddhā hoti āsavānaṁ khayāya.
segs.e: “Mendicants, when a mendicant has three qualities they’re full of joy and happiness in this very life, and they have laid the groundwork for ending the defilements.
What three?

segs.p: Indriyesu guttadvāro hoti, bhojane mattaññū, jāgariyaṁ anuyutto.
segs.e: They guard the sense doors, eat in moderation, and are committed to wakefulness.

segs.p: Kathañca, bhikkhave, bhikkhu indriyesu guttadvāro hoti?
segs.e: And how does a mendicant guard the sense doors?

segs.p: Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu cakkhunā rūpaṁ disvā na nimittaggāhī hoti, nānubyañjanaggāhī;
segs.e: When a mendicant sees a sight with their eyes, they don’t get caught up in the features and details.

segs.p: yatvādhikaraṇamenaṁ cakkhundriyaṁ asaṁvutaṁ viharantaṁ abhijjhādomanassā pāpakā akusalā dhammā anvāssaveyyuṁ. Tassa saṁvarāya paṭipajjati; rakkhati cakkhundriyaṁ; cakkhundriye saṁvaraṁ āpajjati.
segs.e: If the faculty of sight were left unrestrained, bad unskillful qualities of covetousness and displeasure would become overwhelming. For this reason, they practice restraint, protecting the faculty of sight, and achieving its restraint.
When they hear a sound with their ears …
When they smell an odor with their nose …
When they taste a flavor with their tongue …
When they feel a touch with their body …

segs.p: manasā dhammaṁ viññāya na nimittaggāhī hoti nānubyañjanaggāhī;
segs.e: When they know an idea with their mind, they don’t get caught up in the features and details.

segs.p: yatvādhikaraṇamenaṁ manindriyaṁ asaṁvutaṁ viharantaṁ abhijjhādomanassā pāpakā akusalā dhammā anvāssaveyyuṁ, tassa saṁvarāya paṭipajjati; rakkhati manindriyaṁ; manindriye saṁvaraṁ āpajjati.
segs.e: If the faculty of mind were left unrestrained, bad unskillful qualities of covetousness and displeasure would become overwhelming. For this reason, they practice restraint, protecting the faculty of mind, and achieving its restraint.

segs.p: Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, subhūmiyaṁ cātumahāpathe ājaññaratho yutto assa ṭhito odhastapatodo. Tamenaṁ dakkho yoggācariyo assadammasārathi abhiruhitvā vāmena hatthena rasmiyo gahetvā, dakkhiṇena hatthena patodaṁ gahetvā, yenicchakaṁ yadicchakaṁ sāreyyapi paccāsāreyyapi.
segs.e: Suppose a chariot stood harnessed to thoroughbreds at a level crossroads, with a goad ready. A deft horse trainer, a master charioteer, might mount the chariot, taking the reins in his right hand and goad in the left. He’d drive out and back wherever he wishes, whenever he wishes.

segs.p: Evameva kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhu imesaṁ channaṁ indriyānaṁ ārakkhāya sikkhati, saṁyamāya sikkhati, damāya sikkhati, upasamāya sikkhati.
segs.e: In the same way, a mendicant trains to protect, control, tame, and pacify these six senses.

segs.p: Evaṁ kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhu indriyesu guttadvāro hoti.
segs.e: That’s how a mendicant guards the sense doors.

segs.p: Kathañca, bhikkhave, bhikkhu bhojane mattaññū hoti?
segs.e: And how does a mendicant eat in moderation?

segs.p: Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu paṭisaṅkhā yoniso āhāraṁ āhāreti:
segs.e: It’s when a mendicant reflects rationally on the food that they eat:

segs.p: ‘neva davāya, na madāya, na maṇḍanāya, na vibhūsanāya, yāvadeva imassa kāyassa ṭhitiyā, yāpanāya, vihiṁsūparatiyā, brahmacariyānuggahāya, iti purāṇañca vedanaṁ paṭihaṅkhāmi, navañca vedanaṁ na uppādessāmi, yātrā ca me bhavissati, anavajjatā ca phāsuvihāro cā’ti.
segs.e: ‘Not for fun, indulgence, adornment, or decoration, but only to sustain this body, to avoid harm, and to support spiritual practice. In this way, I shall put an end to old discomfort and not give rise to new discomfort, and I will have the means to keep going, blamelessness, and a comfortable abiding.’

segs.p: Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, puriso vaṇaṁ ālimpeyya yāvadeva rohanatthāya, seyyathā vā pana akkhaṁ abbhañjeyya yāvadeva bhārassa nittharaṇatthāya;
segs.e: It’s like a person who puts ointment on a wound only so that it can heal; or who oils an axle only so that it can carry a load.

segs.p: evaṁ kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhu paṭisaṅkhā yoniso āhāraṁ āhāreti:
segs.e: In the same way, a mendicant reflects rationally on the food that they eat:

segs.p: ‘neva davāya, na madāya, na maṇḍanāya, na vibhūsanāya, yāvadeva imassa kāyassa ṭhitiyā, yāpanāya, vihiṁsūparatiyā, brahmacariyānuggahāya, iti purāṇañca vedanaṁ paṭihaṅkhāmi, navañca vedanaṁ na uppādessāmi, yātrā ca me bhavissati, anavajjatā ca phāsuvihāro cā’ti.
segs.e: ‘Not for fun, indulgence, adornment, or decoration, but only to sustain this body, to avoid harm, and to support spiritual practice. In this way, I shall put an end to old discomfort and not give rise to new discomfort, and I will have the means to keep going, blamelessness, and a comfortable abiding.’

segs.p: Evaṁ kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhu bhojane mattaññū hoti.
segs.e: That’s how a mendicant eats in moderation.

segs.p: Kathañca, bhikkhave, bhikkhu jāgariyaṁ anuyutto hoti?
segs.e: And how is a mendicant committed to wakefulness?

segs.p: Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu divasaṁ caṅkamena nisajjāya āvaraṇīyehi dhammehi cittaṁ parisodheti.
segs.e: It’s when a mendicant practices walking and sitting meditation by day, purifying their mind from obstacles.

segs.p: Rattiyā paṭhamaṁ yāmaṁ caṅkamena nisajjāya āvaraṇīyehi dhammehi cittaṁ parisodheti.
segs.e: In the first watch of the night, they continue to practice walking and sitting meditation.

segs.p: Rattiyā majjhimaṁ yāmaṁ dakkhiṇena passena sīhaseyyaṁ kappeti pāde pādaṁ accādhāya sato sampajāno uṭṭhānasaññaṁ manasi karitvā.
segs.e: In the middle watch, they lie down in the lion’s posture—on the right side, placing one foot on top of the other—mindful and aware, and focused on the time of getting up.

segs.p: Rattiyā pacchimaṁ yāmaṁ paccuṭṭhāya caṅkamena nisajjāya āvaraṇīyehi dhammehi cittaṁ parisodheti.
segs.e: In the last watch, they get up and continue to practice walking and sitting meditation, purifying their mind from obstacles.

segs.p: Evaṁ kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhu jāgariyaṁ anuyutto hoti.
segs.e: This is how a mendicant is committed to wakefulness.

segs.p: Imehi kho, bhikkhave, tīhi dhammehi samannāgato bhikkhu diṭṭheva dhamme sukhasomanassabahulo viharati, yoni cassa āraddhā hoti āsavānaṁ khayāyā”ti.
segs.e: When a mendicant possesses these three qualities they’re full of joy and happiness in this very life, and they have laid the groundwork for ending the defilements.”
Linked Discourses 35.240
19. The Simile of the Vipers
The Simile of the Tortoise

segs.p: “Bhūtapubbaṁ, bhikkhave, kummo kacchapo sāyanhasamayaṁ anunadītīre gocarapasuto ahosi.
segs.e: “Once upon a time, mendicants, a tortoise was grazing along the bank of a river in the afternoon.

segs.p: Siṅgālopi kho, bhikkhave, sāyanhasamayaṁ anunadītīre gocarapasuto ahosi.
segs.e: At the same time, a jackal was also hunting along the river bank.

segs.p: Addasā kho, bhikkhave, kummo kacchapo siṅgālaṁ dūratova gocarapasutaṁ.
segs.e: The tortoise saw the jackal off in the distance hunting,

segs.p: Disvāna soṇḍipañcamāni aṅgāni sake kapāle samodahitvā appossukko tuṇhībhūto saṅkasāyati.
segs.e: so it drew its limbs and neck inside its shell, and kept passive and silent.

segs.p: Siṅgālopi kho, bhikkhave, addasa kummaṁ kacchapaṁ dūratova gocarapasutaṁ.
segs.e: But the jackal also saw the tortoise off in the distance grazing.

segs.p: Disvāna yena kummo kacchapo tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā kummaṁ kacchapaṁ paccupaṭṭhito ahosi:
segs.e: So it went up to the tortoise and waited nearby, thinking,

segs.p: ‘yadāyaṁ kummo kacchapo soṇḍipañcamānaṁ aṅgānaṁ aññataraṁ vā aññataraṁ vā aṅgaṁ abhininnāmessati, tattheva naṁ gahetvā uddālitvā khādissāmī’ti.
segs.e: ‘When that tortoise sticks one or other of its limbs or neck out from its shell, I’ll grab it right there, rip it out, and eat it!’

segs.p: Yadā kho, bhikkhave, kummo kacchapo soṇḍipañcamānaṁ aṅgānaṁ aññataraṁ vā aññataraṁ vā aṅgaṁ na abhininnāmi, atha siṅgālo kummamhā nibbijja pakkāmi, otāraṁ alabhamāno.
segs.e: But when that tortoise didn’t stick one or other of its limbs or neck out from its shell, the jackal left disappointed, since it couldn’t find a vulnerability.

segs.p: Evameva kho, bhikkhave, tumhepi māro pāpimā satataṁ samitaṁ paccupaṭṭhito:
segs.e: In the same way, Māra the Wicked is always waiting nearby, thinking:

segs.p: ‘appeva nāmāhaṁ imesaṁ cakkhuto vā otāraṁ labheyyaṁ …pe…
segs.e: ‘Hopefully I can find a vulnerability in the eye,
ear, nose, tongue, body, or
mind.’
That’s why you should live with sense doors guarded.

segs.p: Cakkhunā rūpaṁ disvā mā nimittaggāhino ahuvattha, mā anubyañjanaggāhino.
segs.e: When you see a sight with your eyes, don’t get caught up in the features and details.

segs.p: Yatvādhikaraṇamenaṁ cakkhundriyaṁ asaṁvutaṁ viharantaṁ abhijjhādomanassā pāpakā akusalā dhammā anvāssaveyyuṁ, tassa saṁvarāya paṭipajjatha, rakkhatha cakkhundriyaṁ, cakkhundriye saṁvaraṁ āpajjatha.
segs.e: If the faculty of sight were left unrestrained, bad unskillful qualities of covetousness and displeasure would become overwhelming. For this reason, practice restraint, protecting the faculty of sight, and achieving its restraint.
When you hear a sound with your ears …
When you smell an odor with your nose …
When you taste a flavor with your tongue …
When you feel a touch with your body …

segs.p: manasā dhammaṁ viññāya mā nimittaggāhino ahuvattha, mā anubyañjanaggāhino.
segs.e: When you know an idea with your mind, don’t get caught up in the features and details.

segs.p: Yatvādhikaraṇamenaṁ manindriyaṁ asaṁvutaṁ viharantaṁ abhijjhādomanassā pāpakā akusalā dhammā anvāssaveyyuṁ, tassa saṁvarāya paṭipajjatha, rakkhatha manindriyaṁ, manindriye saṁvaraṁ āpajjatha.
segs.e: If the faculty of mind were left unrestrained, bad unskillful qualities of covetousness and displeasure would become overwhelming. For this reason, practice restraint, protecting the faculty of mind, and achieving its restraint.

segs.p: Yato tumhe, bhikkhave, indriyesu guttadvārā viharissatha, atha tumhehipi māro pāpimā nibbijja pakkamissati, otāraṁ alabhamāno—
segs.e: When you live with your sense doors guarded, Māra will leave you disappointed, since he can’t find a vulnerability,
just like the jackal left the tortoise.
A mendicant should collect their thoughts
as a tortoise draws its limbs into its shell.
Independent, not disturbing others,
quenched: they wouldn’t blame anyone.”
Linked Discourses 35.241
19. The Simile of the Vipers
The Simile of the Tree Trunk (1st)

segs.p: Ekaṁ samayaṁ bhagavā kosambiyaṁ viharati gaṅgāya nadiyā tīre.
segs.e: At one time the Buddha was staying near Kosambī on the bank of the Ganges River.

segs.p: Addasā kho bhagavā mahantaṁ dārukkhandhaṁ gaṅgāya nadiyā sotena vuyhamānaṁ.
segs.e: Seeing a large tree trunk being carried along by the current,
he addressed the mendicants,

segs.p: “passatha no tumhe, bhikkhave, amuṁ mahantaṁ dārukkhandhaṁ gaṅgāya nadiyā sotena vuyhamānan”ti?
segs.e: “Mendicants, do you see that large tree trunk being carried along by the current of the Ganges River?”
“Yes, sir.”

segs.p: “Sace so, bhikkhave, dārukkhandho na orimaṁ tīraṁ upagacchati, na pārimaṁ tīraṁ upagacchati, na majjhe saṁsīdissati, na thale ussīdissati, na manussaggāho gahessati, na amanussaggāho gahessati, na āvaṭṭaggāho gahessati, na antopūti bhavissati;
segs.e: “Mendicants, assume that that tree trunk doesn’t drift toward the near shore or the far shore, or sink in the middle, or get stranded on high ground. And assume that it doesn’t get taken by humans or non-humans or caught up in a whirlpool, and that it doesn’t rot away.

segs.p: evañhi so, bhikkhave, dārukkhandho samuddaninno bhavissati samuddapoṇo samuddapabbhāro.
segs.e: In that case, that tree trunk will slant, slope, and incline toward the ocean.
Why is that?

segs.p: Samuddaninno, bhikkhave, gaṅgāya nadiyā soto samuddapoṇo samuddapabbhāro.
segs.e: Because the current of the Ganges River slants, slopes, and inclines toward the ocean.

segs.p: Evameva kho, bhikkhave, sace tumhepi na orimaṁ tīraṁ upagacchatha, na pārimaṁ tīraṁ upagacchatha;
segs.e: In the same way, assume that you don’t drift toward the near shore or the far shore, or sink in the middle, or get stranded on high ground. And assume that you don’t get taken by humans or non-humans or caught up in a whirlpool, and that you don’t rot away.

segs.p: na majjhe saṁsīdissatha, na thale ussīdissatha, na manussaggāho gahessati, na amanussaggāho gahessati, na āvaṭṭaggāho gahessati, na antopūtī bhavissatha;
evaṁ tumhe, bhikkhave, nibbānaninnā bhavissatha nibbānapoṇā nibbānapabbhārā.
segs.e: In that case, you will slant, slope, and incline toward extinguishment.
Why is that?
Because right view slants, slopes, and inclines toward extinguishment.”

segs.p: Evaṁ vutte, aññataro bhikkhu bhagavantaṁ etadavoca:
segs.e: When he said this, one of the mendicants said to the Buddha:

segs.p: “kiṁ nu kho, bhante, orimaṁ tīraṁ, kiṁ pārimaṁ tīraṁ, ko majjhe saṁsādo, ko thale ussādo, ko manussaggāho, ko amanussaggāho, ko āvaṭṭaggāho, ko antopūtibhāvo”ti?
segs.e: “But sir, what’s the near shore and what’s the far shore? What’s sinking in the middle? What’s getting stranded on high ground? What’s getting taken by humans or non-humans? What’s getting caught up in a whirlpool? And what’s rotting away?”

segs.p: “‘Orimaṁ tīran’ti kho, bhikkhu, channetaṁ ajjhattikānaṁ āyatanānaṁ adhivacanaṁ.
segs.e: “‘The near shore’, mendicant, is a term for the six interior sense fields.

segs.p: ‘Pārimaṁ tīran’ti kho, bhikkhu, channetaṁ bāhirānaṁ āyatanānaṁ adhivacanaṁ.
segs.e: ‘The far shore’ is a term for the six exterior sense fields.
‘Sinking in the middle’ is a term for greed and relishing.
‘Stranded on high ground’ is a term for the conceit ‘I am’.
And what’s getting taken by humans?

segs.p: Idha, bhikkhu, gihīhi saṁsaṭṭho viharati, sahanandī sahasokī, sukhitesu sukhito, dukkhitesu dukkhito, uppannesu kiccakaraṇīyesu attanā tesu yogaṁ āpajjati.
segs.e: It’s when someone mixes closely with laypeople, sharing their joys and sorrows—happy when they’re happy and sad when they’re sad—and getting themselves involved in their business.
That’s called getting taken by humans.
And what’s getting taken by non-humans?

segs.p: Idha, bhikkhu, ekacco aññataraṁ devanikāyaṁ paṇidhāya brahmacariyaṁ carati: ‘imināhaṁ sīlena vā vatena vā tapena vā brahmacariyena vā devo vā bhavissāmi devaññataro vā’ti.
segs.e: It’s when someone leads the spiritual life wishing to be reborn in one of the orders of gods: ‘By this precept or observance or fervent austerity or spiritual practice, may I become one of the gods!’
That’s called getting taken by non-humans.
‘Caught up in a whirlpool’ is a term for the five kinds of sensual stimulation.
And what’s rotting away?

segs.p: Idha, bhikkhu, ekacco dussīlo hoti pāpadhammo asucisaṅkassarasamācāro paṭicchannakammanto assamaṇo samaṇapaṭiñño abrahmacārī brahmacāripaṭiñño antopūti avassuto kasambujāto.
segs.e: It’s when some person is unethical, of bad qualities, filthy, with suspicious behavior, underhand, no true ascetic or spiritual practitioner—though claiming to be one—rotten inside, festering, and depraved.
This is called ‘rotting away’.”

segs.p: Tena kho pana samayena nando gopālako bhagavato avidūre ṭhito hoti.
segs.e: Now at that time Nanda the cowherd was sitting not far from the Buddha.

segs.p: Atha kho nando gopālako bhagavantaṁ etadavoca:
segs.e: Then he said to the Buddha:

segs.p: “ahaṁ kho, bhante, na orimaṁ tīraṁ upagacchāmi, na pārimaṁ tīraṁ upagacchāmi, na majjhe saṁsīdissāmi, na thale ussīdissāmi, na maṁ manussaggāho gahessati, na amanussaggāho gahessati, na āvaṭṭaggāho gahessati, na antopūti bhavissāmi.
segs.e: “I won’t drift toward the near shore or the far shore, or sink in the middle, or get stranded on high ground. And I won’t get taken by humans or non-humans or caught up in a whirlpool, and I won’t rot away.

segs.p: Labheyyāhaṁ, bhante, bhagavato santike pabbajjaṁ, labheyyaṁ upasampadan”ti.
segs.e: Sir, may I receive the going forth, the ordination in the Buddha’s presence?”

segs.p: “Tena hi tvaṁ, nanda, sāmikānaṁ gāvo niyyātehī”ti.
segs.e: “Well then, Nanda, return the cows to their owners.”
“Sir, the cows will go back by themselves, since they love their calves.”
“Still, Nanda, you should return them to their owners.”

segs.p: Atha kho nando gopālako sāmikānaṁ gāvo niyyātetvā yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṁ etadavoca:
segs.e: Then Nanda, after returning the cows to their owners, went up to the Buddha and said to him,
“Sir, I have delivered the cows to their owners.

segs.p: Labheyyāhaṁ, bhante, bhagavato santike pabbajjaṁ, labheyyaṁ upasampadan”ti.
segs.e: May I receive the going forth, the ordination in the Buddha’s presence?”

segs.p: Alattha kho nando gopālako bhagavato santike pabbajjaṁ, alattha upasampadaṁ.
segs.e: And the cowherd Nanda received the going forth, the ordination in the Buddha’s presence.

segs.p: Acirūpasampanno ca panāyasmā nando eko vūpakaṭṭho …pe…
segs.e: Not long after his ordination,

segs.p: aññataro ca panāyasmā nando arahataṁ ahosīti.
